lessons.title: 01 - Abstract and Introduction
lessons.text:
Abstract



Target capture is a common method of generating high throughput DNA sequencing data for phylogenetic reconstruction of species relationships, for which single copy genes are usually most informative. However, a pervasive problem with target capture is that putatively single copy genes may in fact be paralogs resulting from gene duplication, which are problematic for phylogenetic inference because their evolutionary history may differ from the divergence history of species. Here, we use as a case study a target enrichment dataset of 88 species of Detarioideae (Leguminosae) with a focus on the *Sindora* clade to examine approaches for handling paralogs, including the built-in paralog handling functions in HybPiper and CAPTUS, plus subsequent steps using Putative Paralog Detection and the tree-based Yang & Smith orthology inference approach. We compare the paralogs flagged using these methods and verify their performance with BLAST mapping against a reference genome sequence of *Sindora glabra*, and then subsequently compare the species tree topologies produced across these methods. Our comparisons of paralogs flagged across the *Sindora* clade show that the Putative Paralog Detection pipeline was the most accurate in identifying paralogs in terms of its similarity to the BLAST mapping, followed by the built-in paralog identification function of CAPTUS. However, the results we recovered for the Detarioideae subfamily suggest that the largest differences in species tree topology resulted from the use of paralog-filtered alignments (such as with the Putative Paralog Detection pipeline and the Yang & Smith orthology inference approaches) rather than just by removing the sequences of identified paralogous genes. This was true for HybPiper-assembled datasets but was not seen in CAPTUS-assembled datasets. In all comparisons, the topological differences caused by different paralog handling methods tended to be confined to clades where processes such as hybridisation and introgression are prevalent. Our study provides a roadmap to establish the best approach to identify, eliminate or separate paralogs in the absence of a chromosomally contiguous reference genome for a study group, and highlights the importance of careful data inspection and processing in addition to understanding the extent of paralogy and paralog characteristics (e.g., sequence divergence between copies) for their study group.

Introduction



Paralogy is one of the many causes of gene tree conflict, which can interfere with the accurate reconstruction of phylogenetic relationships inferred from DNA sequence data. Paralogs are homologous genes that result from duplication, in contrast to orthologs, which are homologous genes that have arisen by speciation. There are two types of gene duplication which can result in paralog formation: whole genome duplication (WGD), which involves the entire genome, or smaller scale gene duplication events, which include tandem, proximal, dispersed or transposed duplication. Paralogs are common in flowering plants, as WGD events have been recorded in all plant families across the evolutionary history of angiosperms. If cross-species paralogs instead of orthologs are compared, this leads to difficulties in reconstructing phylogenetic relationships, as the evolutionary history of paralogs may not be identical to the evolutionary history of species. The inclusion of paralogous genes and their different evolutionary histories add noise to the phylogenetic signal, which may also affect downstream analyses such as divergence time estimates, biogeographic reconstructions and comparative studies of trait evolution.

1.1. Paralogy in target capture data



Many phylogenetic studies use hybrid capture (target capture) as a reduced-representation genome sequencing approach in which selected putatively single copy genes from one or several reference genomes or transcriptomes are used to generate a 'bait set' that is used to 'capture' the genes of interest across the study group. After the genes have been selected and sequenced, pipelines such as HybPiper or CAPTUS are used to assemble the target sequences.

However, it is difficult to ensure that all the genes are single copy in all the taxa sequenced, because baits are selected based on inferred single copy status in the reference taxa used, but the gene status of other taxa may differ because of other gene or genome duplication events. For this reason, HybPiper and CAPTUS assembly pipelines have subsequent steps to identify and eliminate putative paralogs. There are several other subsequent pipelines for handling paralogs, including Putative Paralog Detection, which is designed to work with HybPiper output. Another is the Target Enrichment Orthology pipeline (hereafter referred to as the Yang & Smith pipeline), which aims to separate paralogs using a phylogenetic tree-based analysis.

1.2. Approaches to paralog handling



The various approaches to handling paralogs can be classified into two main types, which are similarity-based and tree-based methods.

Similarity-based methods pick out potential paralogs based on their sequence identity to the known copy of the gene studied, and these include methods such as the built-in paralog flagging methods of both HybPiper and CAPTUS, along with the subsequent Putative Paralog Detection (PPD) pipeline for HybPiper assemblies. In HybPiper, reference-guided read extraction with BLAST followed by de novo assembly with SPAdes produces the assembled sequences for each gene. Subsequently, the `paralog_retriever` command works by identifying genes for which multiple sequences have been recovered if these are sufficiently long (at least 75% of the reference length). The longest copy is assigned as the main copy, or if the sequence lengths are the same, the sequence with the highest similarity to the reference is assigned to be the main one, while all others are listed as paralogs. In the fully de novo assembly-based pipeline CAPTUS, after sequence assembly with MEGAHIT, sequences are assigned to their respective genes based on their similarity to the reference sequences using BLAT. If multiple sequences are assigned to the same gene, they are ordered based on their similarity and coverage with respect to the reference sequence, and by default the top five paralogs are kept and aligned with the best match (i.e., the main copy), although typically only the main copy will be used for generating phylogenetic trees.

The Putative Paralog Detection (PPD) pipeline works by mapping reads to the HybPiper assembled sequences to generate sequences showing ambiguities (or heterozygosity). If enough taxa share the same heterozygous sites, the gene will be flagged as potentially paralogous because such variability is unlikely to reflect allelic differences, and additional trimming can be carried out to remove regions which have incorporated paralogous reads from the alignments.

In all these similarity-based methods based on HybPiper, CAPTUS and PPD, there are drawbacks. All assume that genes that are not flagged as paralogues are single copy and orthologous, which might not be the case because of hidden orthology, where only one copy of a multicopy gene is present. Hidden orthology can happen because of data processing artifacts such as insufficient sequencing depth or the failure of target capture to recover all copies, or via biological processes such as pseudo-orthology where differential loss after gene duplication leads to the presence of a single but non-orthologous gene copy across species. In addition, all these methods may flag genes as paralogs when in fact the variation is allelic.

Tree-based methods such as the Yang & Smith pipeline use a phylogenetic approach to infer paralogs and orthologs. The Yang & Smith pipeline implements both the "monophyletic outgroups" (MO) and "rooted outgroups" (RT) methods. The MO approach generates a tree with duplicated taxa (i.e., paralogs) removed, while the RT approach retains all separate paralog trees, which allows the evolutionary history of the duplicated gene copies to also be recovered. Tree-based methods allow for allelic variation and true paralogy to be differentiated in duplicated gene copies by removing lineage-specific duplicates in a preprocessing step, but they are dependent on the sequence assembly pipelines such as HybPiper and CAPTUS because these produce the input sequences for the phylogenetic analyses.

Attempts have been made to compare methods of paralog identification and understand the effect of paralogs on phylogenetic inference. While some have found that paralog inclusion has minimal impacts on phylogenetic reconstruction, others have found that paralogs can have a negative impact on species tree topologies and support values. We build on our current understanding of how paralogs affect phylogenetic inference by evaluating the performance of similarity-based methods of paralog detection—including the `paralog_retriever` function of HybPiper, the built-in paralog identification pipeline in CAPTUS and the Putative Paralog Detection pipeline which works on HybPiper-assembled sequences—in comparison to an approach that uses a chromosomal reference genome to identify paralogs with confidence. We then analyse the impact of paralog handling with similarity- and tree-based approaches (MO and RT methods of Yang & Smith) on both coalescent-based and concatenated species trees.

We test these paralog identification pipelines using the *Sindora* clade from subfamily Detarioideae of the legume family (Fabaceae, Leguminosae). The Detarioideae is one of the early-diverging legume subfamilies, with 81 genera and c. 760 species. The *Sindora* clade is part of the Detarieae tribe, which consists of 21 genera, with 11 restricted to Africa, two endemic to Madagascar, two restricted to Asia, and two found only in the Neotropics. The *Sindora* clade consists of five closely related genera: *Sindora*, *Copaifera*, *Tessmannia*, *Sindoropsis*, and *Detarium*. *Sindora* is a genus of 20 species, with 19 species in tropical and subtropical Asia, and one species in West Tropical Africa. *Copaifera* is a pantropical genus of 39 species, with 34 species in South America, four species in Africa and one species in Borneo in Southeast Asia. *Tessmannia*, *Sindoropsis* and *Detarium* are found only in Africa, and they have 24 species, one species and three species respectively. The most recent phylogenetic study of the group has found that the intergeneric relationships among the *Sindora* clade are not well resolved.

We investigate the performance of paralog identification methods through a target capture-based study of the *Sindora* clade using a bait set for the Detarioideae, which was designed based on transcriptome sequences from four Detarioid legumes: *Anthonotha fragrans*, *Afzelia bella*, *Copaifera officinalis* and *Prioria balsamifera*. For each of the four transcriptomes, protein sequence orthology was established by clustering, followed by removing protein sequences present in multiple copies. The remaining protein sequences were further checked for orthology using a phylogenetic approach. As the orthology status of these genes chosen as baits may differ in species other than the four reference transcriptomes used, we verify the paralog status of genes across samples from the *Sindora* clade using the available reference genome of *Sindora glabra*. The *Sindora* clade is an ideal candidate for such a study because the Leguminosae family has experienced several WGD events in its history and there is also one more recent WGD event common to all members of subfamily Detarioideae. Although the bait set was designed for Detarioideae, we expect that across the group diploidisation or localised duplications will have resulted in different copy number variation for many of the target loci across the entire set of species of the *Sindora* clade.

In addition to comparing the paralogs flagged, we also compare the species tree topologies produced by the various paralog handling methods. Our aim is to provide a much-needed comparative assessment of methods for paralog handling in target capture datasets and their impact on the subsequent tree topology, to facilitate the selection of an appropriate pipeline for studies where prior genomic knowledge is scarce.

lessons.title: 02 - Sampling and Sequence Assembly
lessons.text:
Methods



2.1. Sample choice, DNA extraction, target capture and sequencing



A total of 88 samples were sequenced, including 87 from Detarioideae, and one *Cercis canadensis* from the closely related Dialioideae subfamily which was used as the outgroup. Only one sample per species was sampled as this was sufficient to generate an accurate species tree using the coalescent-based phylogenetic inference software ASTRAL, so sampling multiple individuals per species was not necessary. Of the 87 Detarioideae, 25 are from the *Sindora* clade, 47 from other genera in the Detarieae, and 15 from Schotieae, Barnebydendreae, Afzelieae, Amherstieae and Saracaeae.

Different batches of samples were processed in various locations with the details summarised in Supplementary Table 1. For most samples, DNA from fresh, silica-gel dried or herbarium-sampled leaf material was extracted with the CTAB method. The fragment sizes of the genomic DNA extracts were assessed by gel electrophoresis, and where necessary (usually for fresh or recent silica-gel dried leaf material), the genomic DNA was sheared using a Covaris ME-220 focus-ultrasonicator (Covaris Inc., US) to a target fragment size of 350 bp following the manufacturer's protocol. DNA sequencing libraries were prepared with 250 ng of input DNA using the NEBNext Ultra II DNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina with unique dual index adaptors (New England Biolabs, Singapore & New England Biolabs, UK). Target capture was performed with the Detarioideae myBaits kit (Daciel-Arbor Biosciences, US) for 24 h at $60^{\circ}\text{C}$ to enable greater capture of outgroup samples and paralog recovery. For target capture reactions prepared in Singapore, the myBaits kit v.4.01 was used, while for reactions prepared in the UK, the v.5.03 kit was used. For reactions prepared in Belgium, the myBaits kit v.3.0.1 was used.

The sequencing library preparation followed previously established protocols. Paired-end sequencing (150 bp) was performed on an Illumina NextSeq with reagent kit V2 at the GIGA platform (Liège, Belgium). An Illumina NovaSeq was used to generate 150 bp paired-end reads for libraries prepared in Singapore, sequenced by Novogene AIT, and in Exeter, sequenced by the University of Exeter Sequencing Facility.

2.2. Sequence recovery and assembly



2.2.1. HybPiper



Raw reads were trimmed using Trimmomatic v.0.39 with the settings `ILLUMINACLIP: TruSeq3-PE.fa:2:30:10 LEADING:3 TRAILING:3 SLIDINGWINDOW:4:15 MINLEN:25`. A second round of adaptor removal was performed using CUTADAPT v1.14 using the script `more_tidying.sh`. HybPiper v.2.3.0 was used to assemble trimmed and adaptor-free reads using the Detarioideae bait reference fasta file, with the following options: `hybpiper assemble --run_intronerate --chimeric_stitched_contig_check --thresh 70`. The default option of BLAST v.2.13.0 was used for read mapping, with the default coverage cutoff value of 8, and the protein similarity percentage to pull loci of interest (`--thresh`) was raised to 70 from a default of 55 as the closely related Detarioideae sequences were expected to be highly similar to the Detarioideae bait reference. Supercontigs consisting of exons with flanking intron regions were recovered and gathered for downstream analyses. Selected gene alignments were visually checked to identify the presence of chimeric sequences, which have incorporated sequences from two or more gene copies into a single contig. However, these chimeric alignments were not removed to ensure that all analyses were an accurate representation of the pipelines' native ability to deal with paralogs rather than from manual efforts to further clean the alignments.

2.2.2. CAPTUS



Raw reads were provided to the CAPTUS v1.0.1 pipeline for cleaning, de novo assembly, extraction of assembled sequences by gene, and sequence alignment, with parameters modified to match those used by HybPiper. At the step `captus assembly assemble`, the `-min_count` was increased to 8 from the default value of two to match the coverage cutoff in HybPiper. For the step `captus_assembly extract`, the same Detarioideae bait reference fasta file was used, and the protein similarity threshold (`--nuc_min_identity`) was increased to 70 to match that used in HybPiper. In the `captus_assembly align` step, the output containing genes together with their flanking regions (`-formats GF`) was used to match the HybPiper supercontigs. The outgroup *Cercis canadensis* was defined at this step to facilitate sequence alignment. Similar to the HybPiper alignments, selected CAPTUS alignments were also visually inspected for the presence of chimeric assemblies to assess the ability of the respective pipelines to keep paralog sequences separate.

lessons.title: 03 - Paralog Identification Workflows
lessons.text:
2.3. Pipelines for paralog identification and handling



2.3.1. HybPiper paralog retriever



Paralog sequences were recovered with `hybpiper paralog retriever` using default parameters, which identifies a gene as paralogous if multiple sequences more than 75% the length of the reference for that gene are recovered. HybPiper also produces a second paralog warning based on depth, where if the set of sequences assembled have a depth of greater than 1 across at least 75% of the reference length, the gene is identified as paralogous, even if individual sequences are less than 75% the reference length. However, this "paralog warning by depth" was not used as the script only flagged potentially paralogous genes but did not generate paralog sequences for downstream processing. The `hybpiper paralog stats` function was used to summarise and visualise the paralog recovery based on sequence length across all samples. As long as one sample has paralogous sequences recovered, the gene is identified as paralogous in the summary statistics provided by `hybpiper paralog stats`.

2.3.2. CAPTUS



In CAPTUS, paralogs are recovered as part of the default pipeline during the `captus_assembly align` step. All sequences assigned to a gene are aligned and their similarity to the reference sequence was compared. Based on the default paralog handling parameters in CAPTUS (i.e., the `paralog_tolerance` parameter), when more than one sequence was assembled for the gene, the copy with the highest similarity and coverage with respect to the reference was chosen to be the main copy, while up to a total of five other sequences were kept and flagged as paralogs. A summary of the paralogs recovered was provided in the file `captus-assembly_align.paralogs.tsv`.

2.3.3. Putative paralog detection



The Putative Paralog Detection Pipeline (PPD) identifies paralogs by using sequence similarity and the proportion of heterozygous sites. Trimmed reads were mapped back to their assembled sequences, and sequences with an excessively high rate of heterozygosity (> 5% by default) were attributed to assembly errors and removed. The remaining sequences were aligned and if heterozygous sites were shared across more than a certain percentage of samples, the gene was flagged as paralogous.

PPD was run for two different datasets: 1) the 25 *Sindora* clade samples (to allow comparison of paralogs flagged by the BLAST search against the *Sindora glabra* reference genome); and 2) the full dataset of 88 samples across the Detarioideae subfamily (to generate paralog counts for preparing paralog-excluded datasets, and trimmed alignments for subsequent phylogenetic tree construction).

Three values of the `bwa mem` $k$ parameter for read mapping in `Step2.sh` were used to test the impact on paralog identification. This corresponds to the minimum seed length for matches, and we used the recommended value of $k=100$, an intermediate value of $k=60$, and the smallest value of $k=19$, which is the default value for `bwa mem`.

Default values were followed for the subsequent steps of PPD, such that in step s2 sequences with more than 5% of heterozygous sites were removed, in step s6 alignment columns with more than 50% missing data were removed, and in step s7 alignments were further trimmed along a sliding window with parameters `-mi 15` and `-w 20`, where if more than 15 polymorphic sites exist within a sliding window of 20 bp, these polymorphic sites will be marked and removed with TrimAl. However, the number of polymorphic sites was adjusted to be higher than the original maximum of 4 (`-mi 4`) used for single genera. Our datasets of the 25 *Sindora* clade samples and 88 samples across the Detarioideae subfamily were expected to have more variation because they cover greater phylogenetic breadth, so to avoid polymorphic regions from true intergeneric variation from being removed, we increased the value of the `-mi` parameter.

For step s8, genes were identified as paralogous if there were heterozygous sites shared across more than 50% of the samples (the default value, which was used for the set of 25 *Sindora* clade samples). However, a reduced cutoff value of 14%, corresponding to half the size of the *Sindora* clade (13 samples), was used for the full set of 88 samples because heterozygous sites are less likely to be shared across a subfamily as compared to within a single genus. The PPD pipeline generated both a list of putatively paralogous loci along with trimmed alignments where regions of suspected paralogy have been removed. The original scripts were written to run with the output for HybPiper v1.x, and a modified version was created to utilise the output from HybPiper v2.x.

2.3.4. Orthology inference using the Yang & Smith pipeline



The Yang & Smith pipeline infers orthologs (and thus separates paralogs) from the output of target capture pipelines such as HybPiper and CAPTUS. Both the MO and RT methods of the Yang & Smith pipeline work by firstly rooting each gene tree with the outgroups, and next discarding trees with duplications in the outgroups, or that have non-monophyletic outgroups which are nestled within ingroup taxa. Finally, for trees which have passed the filter, the pipeline identifies and prunes the duplicated clades. The MO approach retains only the ortholog tree with the larger number of taxa, with the outgroups included. The RT approach retains all paralogs if they have enough taxa and treats them separately, exporting each without outgroup taxa (which can be added back later for species tree construction).

The original scripts were modified to run in Python 3. Apart from the change in Python version, and a minimum number of 10 taxa for both the MO and RT approaches, all other commands were run with the same parameters. The sample `Sind730_Cercis_canadensis_Rowland_sn` was indicated as the outgroup in the orthology inference step. The script `prune_paralogs_MO_1to1_MO.py` was run as part of the MO approach to first remove trees with non-monophyletic or duplicated outgroups prior to pruning the duplicated taxa from the trees, while for the RT approach the script `prune_paralogs_RT.py` was used to generate trees of each duplicated clade that met the minimum number of 10 taxa.

lessons.title: 04 - Reference Genome Benchmarking
lessons.text:
2.4. Comparison of paralog identification across different methods



We used the reference genome of *Sindora glabra* to identify the number and location of paralogs through a BLAST search using the assembled sequences (both HybPiper and CAPTUS) of taxa from the *Sindora* clade as queries. We limited our BLAST search to just the *Sindora* clade rather than the entire set of species from the Detarioideae clade because this method only detects paralogs present in the reference species *Sindora glabra*, and the results are less accurate the more divergent the taxa are from the reference species. While it is not possible to assess it here, this method could also leave out many potential paralogs from other species in the *Sindora* clade, although there are currently no other reference genomes available within the clade or tribe to allow a more accurate paralog identification across the taxa used here.

For both the HybPiper and CAPTUS-generated assemblies, the BLAST parameters used were `blastn` with an e-value of e-10, chosen to exclude less significant matches. The BLAST output was then filtered to retain only sequences of more than 90 bp in length, removing short matches which are likely to be false or partial. Genes with matches from multiple chromosomes were flagged as paralogous, while those with matches belonging to a single chromosome were manually checked for paralogs mapping to more than one region of the chromosome.

Pairwise comparisons of the paralogs identified with each pipeline (Fig. 1) were made with the respective (HybPiper/CAPTUS-based) BLAST search results. If any of the genes in the pairwise comparisons were not recovered or did not have any significant BLAST matches, the genes were excluded from the pairwise comparisons. These comparisons were represented as confusion matrices with relevant statistics of sensitivity and specificity using the R package `caret` v. 7.0-1.

*Fig. 1. Flowchart of methods used for the comparison of paralogs identified.*

lessons.title: 05 - Species Tree Methods
lessons.text:
2.5. Comparison of species tree topologies



A total of nine comparative analyses were performed, with different combinations of the number of genes included, assembly method, and paralog handling method, to evaluate the impact of these parameters on species tree topologies. These involve using the sequences from the entire set of 88 samples, and the flowchart of all methods is detailed in Fig. 2 and Table 1.

After the sequences were compiled, and paralogs ignored, removed or incorporated, short sequences of less than 25% of the average length were removed, and genes with less than 10 taxa present (out of 88 taxa in total) were removed from the analysis. For each gene, sequences were aligned with MAFFT v7.515 using `-maxiterate 1000`, and alignments were trimmed with TrimAl v1.4.rev15 to remove columns containing more than 75% gaps.

2.5.1. Coalescent-based species tree inference



From the trimmed alignments, gene trees were generated using IQ-TREE v.2.2.2.3 with ModelFinder for automatic model selection and 1000 ultrafast bootstrap replicates. TreeCollapseCL4 v3.0 was used to collapse nodes with less than 10% bootstrap support in the gene trees. TreeShrink v.1.3.9 was also run with default settings, while retaining outgroup tips, to remove tips with unusually long branch lengths which may be the result of misassembled sequences. ASTRAL v.5.7.8 was used to generate the coalescent-based species tree.

2.5.2. Species tree inference from concatenated gene matrix



For each analysis, the post-TreeShrink alignments were concatenated using `AMAS.py` and a concatenated species tree was generated using IQ-TREE with individual genes as the partitions, `MFP + Merge` for the partition selection and 1000 ultrafast bootstrap replicates.

2.5.3. Comparing species tree topologies



To compare the topologies of all trees, the `treespace` v.1.1.4.3 R package was used. `Treespace` uses a combination of topology and branch lengths to represent each phylogenetic tree as points in two-dimensional space. As the branch lengths of the ASTRAL trees and concatenated trees are not comparable, the `nNodes` method, based on the "Steel & Penny tip-tip path difference metric", was used in `treespace` to summarise the trees as a vector based solely on topology, while ignoring branch lengths. Each ASTRAL and concatenated analysis tree file was converted to the newick format and included as one of the inputs to the `treespace` programme.

*Fig. 2. Flowchart of the nine datasets used for comparing the species tree topologies. HybPiper-based datasets are displayed in purple and CAPTUS-based analyses are displayed in green. The labels on the datasets correspond to their order in Table 1.*

**Table 1.** Analyses performed with details on the assembly method and method of paralog handling.

| b) HybPiper RemovedPPD77paralogs | HybPiper | Alignments from the 77 paralogous genes identified by PPD removed

 |
| c) HybPiper PPDdegentrimmed Rem77 | HybPiper | Alignments trimmed by PPD to remove paralogous regions, and removed 77 paralogous genes identified by PPD

 |
| d) HybPiper PPDdegentrimmed | HybPiper | Alignments trimmed by PPD to remove paralogous regions

| e) HybPiper Y&S MO | HybPiper | Assembled sequences processed by the Y&S MO pipeline to retain only orthologous sequences

 |
| i) CAPTUS Y&S RT | CAPTUS | Assembled sequences processed by the Y&S RT pipeline to separate and incorporate paralogous sequences

 |

2.5.4. Assessing support for alternative topologies



Using the ASTRAL tree topology and the concatenated gene alignments, Quartet Sampling v.1.3.1.b was run, using the `raxml-ng` engine and the settings `-reps 100 --threads 4 --lnlike 2`, with the partition file provided to the `-genetrees` parameter. The output included the Quartet Concordance (QC), which measures the extent of gene tree incongruence; Quartet Differential (QD), which indicates if discordant quartets occur in equal proportions, or if one is favoured over the other; and Quartet Informativeness (QI), which assesses if the data was informative enough or if there was a lack of signal. These results were used to determine if poorly supported nodes from bootstrap values or concordance factor analyses were due to a lack of signal, or the presence of conflicting topologies, and if these were due to incomplete lineage sorting or reticulate evolution.

2.5.5. Visualising the topology of all gene trees



To visualise the conflict between all gene trees, DensiTree implemented using the `ggdensitree` command in the R (v. 4.4.2) package `ggtree` was used to plot all rooted gene tree topologies onto the same plot. To keep the length of the trees the same across all gene trees, each gene tree was made ultrametric with the `chronos` function in the `ape` package v.5.8. The DensiTree plots were prepared for all datasets (consisting of 88 taxa each).

2.5.6. Pairwise comparisons of tree topologies



To examine the differences between phylogenetic trees, pairwise comparisons were also made by plotting tanglegrams, where two trees are plotted side by side and differences in the order of the taxa are indicated by lines connecting the two trees. Tanglegrams were made using the `cophylo` function of the R package `phytools` 2.3.0 with individual phylogenetic trees in the newick format as the input. The ASTRAL coalescent-based species trees were used for the tanglegram comparisons as their topology was more consistent than in the concatenated species trees.

lessons.title: 06 - Results: Sequence Recovery and Paralog Detection
lessons.text:
Results



3.1. Summary of sequence recovery from HybPiper and CAPTUS



HybPiper recovered a total of 24,229 genes across all loci and all samples, 2,314 more genes than the 21,915 recovered by CAPTUS for their respective default datasets (Table 2, Supplementary Fig. 1–2). However, CAPTUS tended to recover more variable and parsimony informative sites in the alignments despite the lower number of genes recovered (Table 2).

**Table 2.** Gene Recovery and Alignment Statistics for HybPiper and CAPTUS.

3.2. Comparison of paralog recovery methods using the *Sindora* clade samples



3.2.1. Comparison of number of paralogs recovered from the HybPiper and CAPTUS pipelines



A total of 71 genes were identified as paralogous by HybPiper (Fig. 3). For CAPTUS, 286 genes were found to have paralogs in at least one sample, which are more evenly distributed across the samples and the genes (Fig. 4).

*Fig. 3. Heatmap of paralogs recovered from HybPiper. Each sample occupies one row, and genes are represented by columns. For each sample, genes with paralogs are indicated by dark blue boxes, with darker colours indicating a larger number of paralogs, and the maximum number being 14. The full figure with sample and gene names is available in Supplementary Fig. 3.*

*Fig. 4. Heatmap of paralogs recovered from CAPTUS. Each sample occupies one row, and genes are represented by columns. For each sample, genes with paralogs are indicated by dark blue boxes, with darker colours indicating a larger number of paralogs, and the maximum number being 14. The full figure with sample and gene names is available in Supplementary Fig. 4.*

3.2.2. Paralog identification using the Putative paralog detection (PPD) pipeline



For the set of 25 samples from the *Sindora* clade, with the default value of 50% shared heterozygous sites across gene alignments, the PPD pipeline did not find any paralogous genes at `bwa mem` $k=100$ and only 5 at $k=60$, but found 41 paralogous genes at $k=19$ (Table 3). For the 88 Detarioideae clade samples, when the percentage of shared heterozygous sites was reduced to 14%, `bwa mem` $k=19$ similarly yielded the largest number of paralogous genes (Table 3).

3.4. Assessing accuracy of paralog identification across different methods



PPD showed the closest match in identifying paralogs compared to the BLAST search against the reference genome, followed closely by CAPTUS, despite the large difference in number of paralogous genes identified (41 vs 195) (Table 4). CAPTUS also showed the highest sensitivity in identifying paralogs, followed by PPD and then HybPiper. In terms of specificity, both HybPiper and PPD showed higher specificity than CAPTUS.

Numbers from the four quadrants of each matrix do not add up to the total number of 289 genes as a small number of genes did not have any significant matches in the BLAST search and were excluded.*

lessons.title: 07 - Results: Species Trees and Quartet Sampling
lessons.text:
3.5. Coalescent based and concatenated species trees



For the coalescent-based species trees generated by ASTRAL (Supplementary Figs. 5a–i), topologies were generally well-resolved across all datasets with most of the nodes being well-supported and with a Local Posterior Probability (LPP) score of 95% and above. Most of the nodes with moderate or low support were found within *Daniellia* and *Sindora*, although the node joining the tribes Schotieae and Barnebydendreae was poorly supported in all trees, and several nodes along the phylogenetic backbone were not well supported in the HybPiper PPD-modified and Y&S trees (Supplementary Figs. 5c, d, e, f). Species tree topologies were similar across all methods. Across all ASTRAL trees, topological differences were usually at the species level, for instance among the tips of the genera *Sindora*, *Daniellia*, *Copaifera* and *Guibourtia*. However, for the PPD-trimmed and HybPiper Y&S ASTRAL trees (Supplementary Figs. 5c, d, e, f), the Schotieae and Barnebydendreae tribes were resolved as sister to the rest of the Detarieae tribe as opposed to resolved as sister to the Saraceae, Afzelieae and Amherstieae tribes in all other ASTRAL trees (Supplementary Figs. 5a, b, g, h, i).

The concatenated trees (Supplementary Figs. 6a–i) generated using IQ-TREE produced well-supported phylogenetic trees for all datasets, with almost all nodes with 100% bootstrap support, while nodes with moderate or poor bootstrap support (<75%) were found mainly in *Sindora* and *Daniellia* and nodes subtending the Schotieae and Barnebydendreae tribes. Overall species tree topologies were similar at the backbone and genus level, with the exception of the Schotieae and Barnebydendreae tribes in relation to the other tribes. In the "HybPiper" and "HybPiper RemovedPPD77paralogs" datasets (Supplementary Figs. 6a, b), the Schotieae and Barnebydendreae were resolved as sisters, while in the HybPiper-based datasets with PPD- or Yang & Smith-modified alignments (Supplementary Figs. 6c, d, e, f), Schotieae was resolved as sister to Barnebydendreae which was in turn resolved as sister to the rest of the Detarieae. Finally, for all CAPTUS concatenated trees (Supplementary Figs. 6g, h, i), Barnebydendreae was resolved as sister to the rest of the Detarioideae, followed by Schotieae and then the three tribes Saraceae, Afzelieae and Amherstieae. However, at the species level within *Sindora*, the phylogenetic relationships among the species were more variable in the concatenated trees, with groupings not shared across all nine trees except for the relationships (*Sindora laotica*, *S. glabra*) and (*S. coriacea*, (*S. velutina*, *S. beccariana*)) (Table 5).

3.6. Quartet sampling shows that support for alternative topologies is clustered in certain genera



Across all datasets, most nodes had positive QC values (nodes in green and white) which showed that there were more quartets in agreement than disagreement with the topology (Fig. 6, Supplementary Fig. 7a–i). However, along the phylogenetic backbone for all quartet sampling trees (Supplementary Fig. 7a–i), there were more white nodes ($0 < QC \le 0.5$) than green nodes ($QC > 0.5$), showing that the proportion of concordant quartets did not exceed the discordant quartets by a large majority. Nodes with negative QC values (yellow and red nodes), showing more discordant than concordant quartets, were generally concentrated within the genera *Sindora* and *Daniellia* (Supplementary Fig. 7a–i), within the Amherstieae tribe (Supplementary Fig. 7d) and also along the backbone at nodes leading to the Schotieae and Barnebydendreae (Supplementary Fig. 7d, e).

Quartet Differential (QD) values measure the distribution of the discordant quartets, so the focus was on the yellow and red nodes ($QC < 0$) which had more discordant than concordant quartets. Across all datasets, the QD values of these higher-discordance nodes were closer to 1 than to 0, showing that the discordant quartets tended to be more equally distributed (Supplementary Figs. 7a–i).

Quartet Informativeness (QI) values were generally variable in all datasets, ranging from 1 to close to 0, and nodes with a low proportion of informative replicates were located both along the phylogenetic backbone and also close to the tips of the tree. However, among all the trees, the two PPD-trimmed trees (Supplementary Figs. 7c and d) showed lower QI values when compared to the equivalent branch in the QS results of the other datasets.

*Fig. 6. Quartet sampling results for the dataset "HybPiper", mapped on the ASTRAL phylogenetic tree generated from the "HybPiper" analysis. Circles are colour-coded to reflect Quartet Concordance (QC). Values above branches are scores for Quartet Concordance (QC), Quartet Differential (QD) and Quartet Informativeness (QI), respectively.*

lessons.title: 08 - Results: Gene Trees and Topology Comparisons
lessons.text:
3.7. Visualising the topology of all gene trees for each dataset with DensiTree



The gene trees agreed for most taxa, but within *Sindora*, *Copaifera* and *Daniellia*, the topologies were incongruent. This can be seen in the DensiTree plots, such as in the one for the CAPTUS dataset (Fig. 7, Supplementary Fig. 8a–i), where the topologies for *Sindora*, *Copaifera* and *Daniellia* appear as a diffuse cloud unlike the other genera with clear topologies shared by most gene trees.

*Fig. 7. DensiTree plot showing alternative gene tree topologies for the "CAPTUS" dataset.*

3.8. Visualising differences in overall species tree topologies for various methods and datasets



The largest differences (Axis 1, Fig. 8) in the Treespace plot were due to whether original sequence alignments were used or whether they were modified to have paralogous regions or sequences removed using the PPD trimming or the Y&S pipeline. However, this only applied to the HybPiper-based datasets, and for the CAPTUS datasets the topologies of all datasets were largely similar regardless of whether the alignments were modified as part of the Y&S pipeline. The next largest difference in Axis 2 (Fig. 8) was the split between concatenation-based IQ-TREE species trees and coalescent-based ASTRAL species trees, although the concatenated tree for the dataset "HybPiper_PPDdegentrimmedrem77" was an anomaly in that it appeared close to the other HybPiper PPD-trimmed coalescent-based ASTRAL trees (Fig. 8).

*Fig. 8. Treespace plot across all trees using the "nNodes" method. Concatenated species trees are in green, with HybPiper datasets in light green and CAPTUS datasets in dark green. ASTRAL species trees are in blue, with HybPiper datasets in light blue and CAPTUS datasets in dark blue.*

Species tree topologies compared using tanglegrams were largely similar across key comparisons (Supplementary Figs. 9a–k). In the comparison between the HybPiper dataset and the HybPiper dataset with paralogous genes removed ("HybPiper RemovedPPD77paralogs"), the two trees were completely identical (Supplementary Fig. 9a). For the comparison of the CAPTUS tree with the Yang & Smith-modified CAPTUS trees, the differences were limited to the species level in *Sindora* and *Daniellia*. However, in the comparisons of the HybPiper with the PPD- or Yang & Smith-modified datasets, there were differences at the tribe level relationships between Schotieae and Barnebydendreae (Supplementary Figs. 9b, c, d, e).

The comparison of HybPiper and CAPTUS-generated trees (Supplementary Fig. 9h) showed that the trees were highly similar with only species-level differences in *Sindora*. When ASTRAL and concatenated tree topologies were compared with each other (Supplementary Figs. 9i, j, k), the differences involved both species-level changes in genera such as *Sindora*, *Tessmannia*, *Guibourtia*, and also at the tribe level involving the placement of Schotieae and Barnebydendreae.

lessons.title: 09 - Discussion: Comparing Paralog Methods
lessons.text:
Discussion



4.1. Comparing paralogs flagged across methods



We used the *Sindora glabra* reference genome to verify the paralog status of the genes studied and compared other similarity-based methods of paralog detection using this information. We consider this reference genome approach to be the most objective and replicable benchmark currently available, but it may be the case that the paralog status of different species may differ from the reference, especially as species are more evolutionarily distant from it, or that paralogous gene copies may not have been successfully recovered. To mitigate this issue of phylogenetic distance from our *Sindora glabra* reference genome, we limited our comparisons of paralogs identified to taxa within the *Sindora* clade. The reference genome approach contrasts with the other methods of paralog detection studied here, which make use of "in-silico" characteristics such as heterozygosity or gene tree topologies. Other studies comparing the accuracy of paralog detection methods used visual observation of gene alignments to estimate the true paralog status, which has the potential to introduce a certain degree of subjectivity in the paralog assignments.

4.1.1. Built-in paralog identification scripts from assembly pipelines



CAPTUS flagged more potential paralogs than HybPiper (Figs. 3 & 4), but not all of these may be true paralogs, because they may instead be alleles. The greater recovery of genes with paralogs in CAPTUS could be due to the completely de novo read assembly compared to HybPiper's partially reference-guided approach. CAPTUS may therefore allow more divergent or low coverage paralog sequences to be recovered, reducing the incidence of "artifactual orthologs" where the "differential assembly of copies in a multicopy gene results in the recovery of non-orthologous sequences for a given locus across taxa". In HybPiper, the paralog reads may also have been sequenced but incorporated into the sequences of the main copies, generating chimeric sequences in the process (Supplementary Fig. 10A). Chimeric sequences refer to assemblies which contain sequence data from more than one gene copy, for instance by stitched contigs where exons of different copies are combined to produce the final assembly, and alternatively by "over-lumping", where two or more copies of the same gene or exon are used to produce the final assembly which contains sequence variation from each copy used. Chimeric sequences were also present in the CAPTUS output, but to a lesser extent than HybPiper (Supplementary Fig. 10B).

4.1.2. PPD-based methods



When compared to the paralogs flagged using HybPiper and CAPTUS, PPD run on the HybPiper assembled sequences was the most accurate in terms of its similarity to the results of the reference genome-guided BLAST search, although this was followed closely by CAPTUS. The similarity in accuracy was unexpected given the large difference in number of paralogous genes flagged by PPD and CAPTUS (41 vs 195) from samples within the *Sindora* clade. The PPD method was less sensitive than CAPTUS because it did not find as many genes with paralogs, but was highly specific. That is, genes identified as paralogous through PPD were also found to be paralogous based on the BLAST search. CAPTUS, on the other hand, found many putatively paralogous genes, but some of these were not identified as paralogous according to the BLAST search. While some of them could be orthologous genes rather than genes with paralogs, it is also possible that these "false positives" from CAPTUS were in fact paralogs in non-*Sindora* taxa because the BLAST search is based only on the single reference species *Sindora glabra*.

While PPD was more accurate in terms of similarity in paralog flagging to the BLAST search compared to HybPiper and CAPTUS, we had to modify several of the PPD running parameters to suit our two study groups of the *Sindora* clade and the Detarioideae subfamily. Both of these have a broader taxonomic spread than the genus-level analyses carried out in the original PPD paper. Firstly, we modified the `bwa-mem` $k$-value from the default of 100 to 19, which allowed more potentially paralogous genes to be flagged (Table 3), by allowing reads from both the main gene copy and also the paralogs to be mapped. Higher values of $k$ (such as $k=100$) might be useful for paralogs which differ in just a few nucleotides, whereas the paralogs within the Detarioideae or the *Sindora* clade exhibit larger differences (e.g., longer indels or more SNPs) where paralog reads could be excluded with such a high $k$ value. *Castanea* (Fagaceae), previously used as an exemplar, is a genus with a history of small-scale genome duplications, whereas in Detarioideae there is a whole genome duplication event common to the entire subfamily. The difference in time scale for these duplication events, and the selection pressures exerted on the duplicated genes, would differ between *Castanea* and Detarioideae, resulting in different paralog characteristics.

PPD can be an effective method for finding paralogous genes provided that the parameters are suited to the taxonomic span of the dataset and with a suitable `bwa mem` $k$ value for the nature of paralogs present in the data. With the default parameters, the pipeline did not manage to identify any paralogs at all (Table 3), which was unusual given that both the default HybPiper and CAPTUS pipelines identified much higher numbers of genes with paralogs. We suggest that as a first pass, the number of paralogs identified from HybPiper or CAPTUS can be used to guide the optimisation of parameters for running PPD.

lessons.title: ortologous
lessons.text: *Miren, muchachos, las palabras en biología pesan. Decir 'ortólogo' suena a verdad ontológica: genes separados por pura especiación*[1]*. Pero seamos honestos: en bioinformática, 'ortólogo' es muchas veces un* **término sombrilla** *, un constructo operacional ante la incertidumbre*[2]*. Cuando un pipeline nos dice 'encontré el ortólogo', lo que realmente dice es 'esta fue la única copia que pude ensamblar'*[2]*. Pero por debajo se pueden esconder 'ortólogos artifactuales', quimeras o duplicaciones borradas por el tiempo*[2][3]*. Por eso, la verdadera filosofía filogenómica no es solo correr programas, sino interrogar nuestro vocabulario: ¡un ortólogo operacional no siempre es un ortólogo evolutivo!*

lessons.title: 10 - Discussion: Recommendations and Conclusion
lessons.text:
4.2. Comparing species tree topologies across methods



From the "treespace" plot (Fig. 8), the species tree topologies tended to cluster into groups first based on whether their alignments were paralog-filtered, either through the additional trimming done by the PPD pipeline or by the Yang & Smith pipeline, although this effect was only seen for HybPiper-based analyses and not the CAPTUS-based analyses. The topological instability in these HybPiper-based trees, along with the lower paralog recovery in HybPiper (Figs. 3 & 4), could be caused by the stochastic nature of paralog recovery in HybPiper, insufficient sequencing depth, or the assembly of "chimeric sequences". The next strongest determinant of species tree topologies was whether the trees were constructed using the ASTRAL coalescent-based or a concatenation-based method.

Across all tanglegram comparisons (Supplementary Figs. 9a–k), tree topologies were similar, except for a few occasions where differences occurred on some backbone nodes or within a few genera which indicate areas of true biological incongruence rather than a lack of data. Genera such as *Sindora* and *Daniellia*, and the Schotieae and Barnebydendreae tribes often have branches with low Quartet Concordance (QC) scores (Fig. 6, Supplementary Fig. 7a–i), which shows high incongruence among gene trees in these genera and tribes, regardless of dataset. QD values close to 0 show a skewed distribution of alternative quartets, suggesting introgression or hybridisation, and QD values close to 1 show more equally distributed discordant quartets, indicative of the random process of incomplete lineage sorting (ILS). Across all datasets, regardless of paralog handling, QD values in *Sindora* and *Daniellia* often ranged between 0 and 1, which suggests both ILS and the possibility of reticulate evolution. In addition, the relationships of the tribes Schotieae and Barnebydendreae are known to be unstable and can change depending on whether plastome or nuclear DNA is used, which may reflect the presence of ancient hybridisation.

The Quartet Informativeness (QI) values were the lowest in the two datasets with the PPD trimmed alignments (`HybPiper PPDdegentrimmed`, `HybPiper PPDdegentrimmedrem77`) (Supplementary Figs. 7c, d), which shows that the trimming of paralogous regions led to a decrease in informative characters for species tree construction. Nevertheless, the species tree topologies were generally consistent, with any differences restricted to the same genera and deeper nodes as in the other tree comparisons (Supplementary Figs. 9b, c).

The presence of ILS and potential hybridisation is further suggested by the DensiTree plots (Fig. 7, Supplementary Fig. 8a–i) where there is a lack of a clear consensus topology for *Sindora*, *Copaifera* and *Daniellia*. This is observed in all datasets regardless of the method of paralog handling, which shows that the signal of ILS and possible hybridisation persists despite our best efforts to exclude or separate paralogs.

4.3. Recommendations for paralogy detection



Overall, the following recommendations are given to guide choice of paralog detection in the absence of a reference genome or prior genomic knowledge for the study group, although the choice of method will be influenced by the taxonomic breadth, history of WGD, and paralog characteristics in the study group. Firstly, in deciding between which assembly pipeline to use, CAPTUS performs better at recovering all possible paralogous gene copies compared to HybPiper and reduces the incidence of "artifactual orthologs", where a multi-copy gene only has a single copy recovered because of insufficient sequencing depth, assembly settings and divergent probes, although the last reason is less likely here due to the use of taxon-specific Detarioideae baits. Across all methods of paralog detection, the heterozygosity-based method PPD was the most accurate, albeit just slightly more so than the built-in paralog detection in CAPTUS, although the default parameters need to be optimised for each dataset. A similar heterozygosity-based method, HybPhaser, was also tested with similarly positive results. These methods allow the identification of genes with paralogs and their exclusion from further analyses, which is a commonly used method to ensure the dataset contains single copy genes. In our case study the removal of paralogous genes did not lead to large changes in species tree topology, which suggests that the phylogenetic signal is stronger than the noise from including paralogous sequences.

In all the similarity-based paralog detection methods, there is no completely objective way of differentiating true paralogs from just allelic variation. Additionally, an indication of potential paralogy from any of the similarity-based methods may not necessarily mean that multiple gene copies were successfully recovered. Tree-based methods such as the Yang & Smith pipeline provide an alternative to distinguish alleles from paralogs that can be separated for use in subsequent species tree construction. As our dataset involves a history of whole genome duplication leading to many duplicated genes and extensive paralogy, the most theoretically sound method would be to use an assembly pipeline to recover as many gene copies and as few chimeric sequences as possible and then use the Yang & Smith tree-based approach to sort gene copies into their respective paralogs, which can then be treated separately as individual orthologs when generating species trees. In our case we would recommend the use of CAPTUS over HybPiper because of its higher paralog recovery rates, although this may depend on the study group.

Conclusion



In this case study using Detarioideae legume clades, the best method for identifying paralogs in the absence of a reference genome was through PPD. However, this method is currently only designed to be used with sequences assembled with HybPiper and requires optimised parameters that relate to the taxonomic breadth of the study group. The next most accurate method is the default paralog identification methods of CAPTUS which recovered more paralogous genes than HybPiper. PPD and the default paralog detection in HybPiper and CAPTUS are useful for identifying genes with paralogs to exclude them from further analyses. However, if the aim is to separate the various paralog copies and produce individual gene trees for each copy recovered, short of having a reference genome for the study group, we would recommend using the Yang & Smith RT approach on CAPTUS-generated data.

Whilst different methods of handling paralogues resulted in datasets of different sizes and non-identical sets of genes from the Detarioideae bait set, the resulting species trees were largely similar topologically. Any differences may reflect areas of the topology affected by real biological issues such as ILS and reticulation. It seems that for the Detarioid legumes, the genes represented in the bait set provide sufficient common phylogenetic signal that emerges across diverse methods of paralogy handling. However, this may differ across bait sets used and taxonomic groups studied and we encourage future empirical studies comparing approaches to paralog detection in target capture DNA sequence data from other plant clades.

lessons.title: filoexponetyps-script
lessons.text:
¿Juzgar por la pinta o buscar el árbol familiar?
*(Entra con actitud relajada, sonriendo, haciendo un gesto amplio con las manos hacia el público)*

**"¡Ey, parces! Oigan pues.** Después de escuchar a mis compañeros meterle la ficha a cómo atrapamos las secuencias en el laboratorio, a mí me toca la parte que me trasnocha y me apasiona: **la filosofía de la reconstrucción filogenética**.

A ver, metámonos en el cuento con una pregunta filosófica: cuando buscamos genes homólogos, ¿cómo sabemos quién es quién? Aquí hay dos grandes escuelas. Por un lado están los **métodos de similitud** *(similarity-based)*. Eso es básicamente juzgar por la pinta: si dos secuencias de ADN se parecen un montón en su código o comparten cierta heterocigosis, asumimos que son hermanitas ortólogas. 

Pero ¡ojo al gol! En biología la apariencia engaña. Ahí es donde entran los **métodos basados en árboles** *(tree-based)*. Esos no se quedan con la foto del momento; se van al registro civil evolutivo. Construyen el árbol genealógico completo para ver si esa duplicación ocurrió ayer o hace millones de años. ¡Es pasar de la mera apariencia a la verdadera genealogía!"


Paralog Identification Workflows (La filogenia al rescate)

"Entonces, ¿cómo desenredamos esa vaca loca de los parálogos cuando no tenemos un genoma de referencia a la mano? 

Entran a la cancha flujos de trabajo basados en árboles como el de **Yang & Smith**. ¿Y cómo camella esa herramienta? Fácil: primero enraíza cada árbol de gen usando un grupo externo —nuestro *outgroup*. Luego detecta dónde ocurrieron las duplicaciones de genes y empieza a podar. 

Tiene dos sabores bien bacanos: 
El método **MO** *(Monophyletic Outgroups)*, que se queda solo con el sub-árbol ortólogo que tenga más especies.
Y el método **RT** *(Rooted Outgroups)*, que es mi favorito filosófico. RT no bota los parálogos a la basura; los separa y los trata como linajes independientes. O sea, ¡no ignora la duplicación genómica, sino que la integra a la historia evolutiva como un locus nuevo!"


Species Tree Methods (¿Concatenar o Coalescer?)
*(Hace una pausa dramática, mirando al público con curiosidad intelectual)*

"Con esos datos limpios, pasamos a inferir el **árbol de especies** *(Species Tree)*. Y aquí se arma otro debate ontológico sabroso: **¿Concatenación vs. Coalescencia?**

Por un lado, la **concatenación** —usando programas como *IQ-TREE* con *ModelFinder*— agarra todos los genes, los pega en una sola matriz gigante y asume que hay un supergen matriz que dicta la historia. 

Por el otro lado, la **coalescencia multisitio** —con *ASTRAL*— reconoce que cada gen tiene su propio árbol y su propia micro-historia evolutiva. *ASTRAL* entiende que fenómenos como la **ordenación incompleta de linajes** *(Incomplete Lineage Sorting o ILS)* hacen que el árbol de un gen no siempre sea idéntico al árbol de la especie. Es democratizar la voz de los genes, parce: ¡cada locus aporta su señal!"


Results: Species Trees y Quartet Sampling
*(Con tono de entusiasmo científico, usando las manos para enfatizar los resultados)*

"¿Y qué nos dijeron los resultados en el clado *Sindora* y la subfamilia Detarioideae?

Para evaluar la solidez de los nodos, no nos quedamos solo con el *bootstrap*. Usamos **Quartet Sampling**. Esta belleza nos da tres métricas clave:
**QC** *(Quartet Concordance)*: si los cuartetos de genes apoyan la rama.
**QD** *(Quartet Differential)*: si las topologías en conflicto son parejas o sesgadas.
**QI** *(Quartet Informativeness)*: si hay buena información o puro ruido.

¿Y qué pillamos? Que la gran mayoría de los nodos del árbol salieron firmes, con QC positivo (nodos verdes). Pero en géneros bravos como *Sindora* y *Daniellia*, los valores de QC bajaron. Y lo más interesante: el QD estuvo cerca de 1. ¿Eso qué traduce en cristiano? Que la discordancia no es error metodológico; es biología pura. Hay una mezcla entre ILS e introgresión o hibridación antigua en esas leguminosas."



"Para rematar, visualizamos esa selva de árboles. Cuando tiras todos los árboles de genes en un gráfico de **DensiTree**, en *Sindora* y *Copaifera* no ves una línea clara, sino una nube difusa de ramas entrelazadas. ¡La firma inconfundible de la complejidad biológica!

Y al comparar todas las topologías con **Treespace** usando la métrica *nNodes*, descubrimos la joya de la corona del estudio: en los datos de *HybPiper*, las mayores diferencias en el árbol de especies vinieron de filtrar los alineamientos con PPD o Yang & Smith, más que de remover los 77 genes paralógos completos. En cambio, en *CAPTUS*, las topologías fueron súper estables y consistentes, sin importar cómo manejaras los parálogos.

**¿La conclusión filosófica, mi gente?** Los genes no leen nuestros manuales de bioinformática. Pero a pesar de los parálogos y la hibridación, la señal filogenómica del clado *Sindora* es tan potente que emerge clara y firme por encima de cualquier ruido. ¡Muchas gracias!"
